newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU states positive on single market action plan.
newsitem.headline: EU states positive on single market action plan.

text.p: European Union member states are expected to take a largely positive initial view of the European Commission's ambitious action plan to complete the bloc's single market by the same time monetary union starts.
The EU executive last month adopted a first draft of the plan to build a truly internal market in the 15-nation bloc by 1999. It will be debated by EU internal market ministers on Wednesday.
"Generally there is a favourable welcome to it," one EU diplomat said on Friday.

But there were also member states which felt that the Commission's draft was "a bit on the ambitious side," he said, referring for example to well-known difficulties in the past to agree on more tax harmonisation.
"The devil is in the detail," another EU official said. "Everybody has their own shopping list."

The European Commission, saying the single market is closely linked with economic and monetary union (EMU), seeks ministers' comments before its final adoption of the plan, which will then be presented to EU leaders meeting in Amsterdam on June 16-17.

The Commission launched the original single market programme in 1985 to create a huge domestic market to help European firms compete on world markets. To keep up the pressure, the EU set a December 31, 1992 deadline for completing it and almost made it.
However, some of the most controversial and complicated issues -- such as greater tax harmonisation and the abolition of border controls on people -- were left unresolved.
EU Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti insists on the need to plug existing holes in the single market.

His plan aims to remove remaining barriers to the free movement of goods, services, capital and people across national borders -- seen as essential if the EU is to catch up with economic rivals the United States and Japan.

"We have no choice but to follow through if we want a single market that delivers more growth, more innovation, more jobs, improved living and working conditions and a wider choice of quality products and services at lower prices, as well as greater personal freedom for our citizens," he said last month.
There were still many distortions within the single market such as different tax regimes which harmed fair competition.
Unless action was taken, cross-border capital flows to avoid high taxes on capital income would intensify with EMU as foreign exchange risks disappeared, Monti added.

Besides taxation, the plan will seek to break down barriers in the energy market and the pension funds industry and to create an European company statute -- controversial proposals which the EU has failed to agree on in the past.

Apart from these legislative measures, the plan focuses on the implementation and enforcement of existing single market legislation. "Member states must close the gap between what they say and what they do concerning the single market," Monti said.

According to a survey published by the Commission last year, the single market has resulted in up to 900,000 more jobs, an increase in EU income of 1.1-1.5 percent, and a lowering of inflation rates of 1.0-1.5 percent.
